rejected.title: Language and identity
card: The words we choose show who we are. They can hint at where we live, how old we are and which groups we belong to. Sharing a group's words can help people feel they belong.
Slang
informal words used mostly among friends or people of a similar age, such as "sick" to mean great.
Local saying
a word or phrase used mainly in one place or region, such as "port" for a school bag, which many people say in Queensland.
Idiom
a phrase whose meaning is not the same as its separate words, such as "under the weather" for feeling unwell.

a.q: Jai tells his mates that a new skateboard trick was "mad", meaning excellent. What kind of language is this?
opts: Slang, used informally among friends
An idiom, a phrase with a hidden meaning
A local saying used only in one town
A formal word chosen for a school essay
a.why: Using "mad" to mean excellent is informal language shared by a group of friends, so it is slang. It is not an idiom, because an idiom is a fixed phrase and not a single word with a new meaning.
a.clue: Think about who Jai is talking to.

b.q: Priya moves from Perth to a new school in Darwin and starts using the phrases her new classmates use. What does this most likely show?
opts: She is using shared words to feel part of a group
She is using words that have no link to identity
She has forgotten how to speak in a formal way
She is using idioms, which only adults say
b.why: People often take on the words of a group to fit in and show they belong. It does not mean she cannot speak formally, because speakers can change their words to suit who they are talking to.
b.clue: Why might someone copy the way a new group talks?

problems.detail: "Arvo" is used across Australia and is usually classed as Australian slang, so it is a weak example of a local saying "used mainly in one place or community". Students could then struggle to tell slang from local sayings. A truly regional word would work better, such as "bubbler" or "port" for a school bag in Queensland.
The general point "Using shared words can help people feel they belong" sits inside the idiom bullet, so it reads as if it applies only to idioms. It should be its own line.
The clue "informal words shared by friends" echoes the wording of the right option ("used informally among friends"), so students can match the words without knowing the idea.
The clue "Shared words can help people belong" repeats the right option almost word for word ("using shared words to feel part of a group"), which gives the answer away.
